messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

For forty years, Amir had been the one arriving at scenes of chaos and bringing a measure of calm. At sixty-one, he was one of the most experienced paramedics in his unit, a man defined by his competence under pressure. That sense of self began to fracture six months ago, during a late-night call-out to a suburban house. The dispatch was for an unconscious male. He and his partner found the man in a cramped, windowless basement, surrounded by canisters and makeshift chemical apparatus. The air was thick with a sharp, cloying smell—part industrial solvent, part cheap alcohol. As they moved to intubate, Amir’s partner stumbled, knocking over a container. A colourless vapour hissed out. Before he could react, Amir took a breath and felt a sudden, searing fire in his lungs. The world narrowed to a desperate, panicked fight for air in the suffocating dark. He was certain, in that moment, that he was dying.

The physical recovery was slow, but the psychological aftermath has been relentless. The trauma did not stay in the basement; it now lives in his daily life, triggered by the most mundane cues. Back at the station a month after the incident, his partner cleaned a small cut with an alcohol swab. The scent hit Amir like a physical blow, and without warning, he was no longer in the brightly lit breakroom but back in the suffocating dark, the memory of his burning lungs so vivid he gasped for air. This is the nature of the memory for him: it arrives unbidden, a sensory ambush that brings with it the same raw terror he felt on the basement floor. Because the memory feels so real and can overpower him without warning, he has begun to scan his environment constantly for anything that might contain a piece of it; any confined space, any sharp chemical odour, even the dim light of an evening room, now feels like a potential precursor to the terror. The sight of his own workplace, the very ambulance he once commanded with pride, now fills him with a profound sense of dread, forcing him to take an extended leave of absence.

The sheer terror of these flashbacks has become something to be managed at all costs, and Amir’s life has reorganised itself around this single, desperate goal. He had come to believe that if he were ever alone, the memories would consume him entirely. To prevent this, he began to keep himself constantly surrounded by people, filling his days with visits from his adult sons and clinging to his wife, Sameera, in the evenings, a strategy that has begun to strain her patience. When the memories do break through, he feels so overwhelmed by the wave of emotion that he has to shut it down immediately, often by launching into a frantic, detailed rumination about the call. He spends hours replaying the moments in the basement, meticulously dissecting every decision, convinced that if he could just identify the one thing he should have done differently—waited for the hazmat team, worn better gear—he could somehow contain the memory’s power.

This constant mental rehearsal, meant to provide a sense of control, only seems to etch the memory deeper, making it more vivid and easier to trigger. His avoidance, intended to protect him, instead makes the world outside his home feel more menacing and saturated with threats. The more he avoids hospitals and the sight of ambulances, the more potent they become as symbols of his failure and terror. The cycle has become ruthlessly efficient. A trigger, like the darkness of a movie theatre, can instantly bring back the full memory. The terror of the memory then fuels his drive to avoid such situations and to ruminate on what he could have done to prevent the event. In turn, this rumination keeps the memory sharp and powerful, which sensitises him further to his triggers. His world has become a map of things to be avoided, a landscape where the smell of rubbing alcohol or the sight of his own uniform can detonate a memory he cannot bear.

It was Sameera who finally brought him to therapy. She told him, gently but firmly, that she felt like she was losing him, not to the chemical exposure, but to the ghost of it. Amir is now on the verge of being forced into early retirement, a prospect that terrifies him almost as much as the memory itself. He feels like a failure, a shell of the capable man he once was. He came to the first session with a simple, desperate hope: to be able to sit alone in his own living room again without being afraid of his own mind.
